clue.text: Executive client's luggage

blocks.note: a suit is slang for a business executive, from the clothes they wear
a client of a social worker or lawyer is a case; with the possessive 's that becomes CASE'S

explanation.surface: Someone notices that the bags belong to a businessperson's client.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as a possessive phrase, but the 's simply supplies the final S, apostrophe ignored as crosswords allow.
explanation.definitionFit: Suitcases are the cases travellers pack, so they are a common kind of baggage.

clue.text: Opportunistic spongers in outskirts of Enfield see squat being wrecked

indicators.note: the outskirts of a town are its edges, so only the outer letters of the word are kept
something wrecked is smashed up, so the letters lose their original order

blocks.note: the first and last letters of the London borough
taken as written, as anagram material

explanation.surface: Freeloaders in north London watch a squatted building being trashed.
explanation.walkthrough: Squeegee bandits are people who wash car windscreens uninvited at traffic lights and then demand money. 'Spongers' is a pun, since a squeegee and sponge are their tools.
explanation.definitionFit: These windscreen washers pester stopped drivers for cash, so they are cadgers taking a chance, idiomatically scroungers.

clue.text: Recurrence of mastoiditis renders one senseless

indicators.note: a recurrence is a running back again, so the letters are read in the opposite direction
the answer is made of letters belonging to the following word, sitting inside it

blocks.note: the letters in the middle of the ear infection's name, after MAS and before TIS

explanation.surface: A relapse of a nasty ear infection leaves the patient unable to feel or hear.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Senseless' looks medical, as if the patient has lost hearing, but it means foolish. Mastoiditis is an infection of the bone behind the ear.
explanation.definitionFit: A fool lacks common sense, so a person with no wits is described in everyday speech as an idiot.

clue.text: Man runs into sea that's polluted densely wooded area

indicators.note: going into something puts it inside, so one piece is placed within another

blocks.note: a chap is an informal word for a man

the Aral Sea in Central Asia, notoriously shrunken and polluted

explanation.surface: A man wades into a filthy sea, apparently an environmental story.
explanation.walkthrough: The Aral Sea is famous for its pollution and shrinkage, which makes 'polluted' a description of that sea rather than an anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Chaparral is thick scrubby vegetation of dwarf oaks and shrubs in California and similar dry regions.

clue.text: Last two letters in listed novel written in non-naturalistic way

indicators.note: novel means new and different, so the material is given a fresh arrangement

blocks.note: the last two letters of the alphabet
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone compares the closing letters of a novel on a reading list with its unusual prose.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Last two letters' reads as the end of some word, but means the end of the alphabet; 'novel' looks like a book.
explanation.definitionFit: Stylized art or writing follows conventions and mannerisms rather than imitating reality closely.

clue.text: Questionnaire makes us very confused

indicators.note: confused things are muddled, so the letters are jumbled out of order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A complaint that a form is baffling to fill in.
explanation.walkthrough: The complaint about a baffling form hides the instruction: 'confused' tells you to rearrange the two little words before it.
explanation.definitionFit: A survey is a set of questions put to many people to gather opinions or facts.

clue.text: Rock regularly puncturing jeep wheels

indicators.note: regularly means at even intervals, so every other letter is taken

blocks.note: the first, third, fifth, seventh and ninth letters

explanation.surface: A stone keeps getting into the tyres of an off-road vehicle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rock' looks like the stone doing the puncturing, but it is slang for a gem, especially a diamond.
explanation.definitionFit: In slang a rock is a precious stone such as a diamond, and a gem is a jewel.

clue.text: Gently push head out from under jay's beak

indicators.note: with the head out, the leading letter is removed
in a down entry, coming from under something means sitting below it

blocks.note: jay is the sound of the letter J when said aloud, its spelt-out name
to nudge is to push gently

explanation.surface: Advice on nudging your head out from under a bird's beak.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jay's beak' looks like the bird's bill, but 'jay' is the letter J and 'beak' is the definition: British slang for a magistrate or judge.
explanation.definitionFit: Beak is old British slang for a magistrate or schoolmaster, someone who sits in judgment.

clue.text: Without oxygen we go blue

indicators.note: in its old sense without means outside, so one piece wraps round another

blocks.note: O is the chemical symbol for oxygen
taken as written
'Begone!' is an old command meaning go away

explanation.surface: Deprived of oxygen, we turn blue in the face.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Without' reads as lacking, but here it has its archaic sense of outside; 'blue' looks like a skin colour but means sad.
explanation.definitionFit: Feeling blue is feeling sad, and woebegone describes a miserable, sorrowful look.

clue.text: Quick to appreciate those who appreciate performance

definitions.note: adjective; the answer is an adverbial phrase meaning very quickly

definitions.text: to appreciate those who appreciate performance

blocks.note: first meaning: a British idiom for very fast

blocks.clueFragment: to appreciate those who appreciate performance
blocks.note: second meaning, taken literally: to be fond of the people applauding a show

explanation.walkthrough: Like the clappers is British slang for at great speed. Read word by word, it is to like (appreciate) the clappers, the audience members who applaud.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom, probably from a bell's clapper swinging fast, means rapidly, while literally it is enjoying applauders.

clue.text: Rain flowing into lead-free sink connected to waterworks

indicators.note: something flowing is fluid and moving, so the letters run into a new order
free of its lead means without its first letter
going into something puts it inside, so one piece is placed within another

blocks.note: taken as written, as anagram material
to sink something in the ground is to bury it

explanation.surface: Rainwater pours into an unleaded sink plumbed into the water supply.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Waterworks' looks like plumbing, but it is a jokey British euphemism for the bladder and urinary system.
explanation.definitionFit: Waterworks is humorous slang for the body's bladder and kidneys, so the adjective means relating to urine.

clue.text: Guzzle wine in the van like white trash

indicators.note: the van is the vanguard, the front, so this piece leads the other

blocks.note: red is red wine
to neck a drink is British slang for gulping it down

explanation.surface: Someone swigging cheap wine in the back of a van is dismissed as trailer-park types.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Van' looks like a vehicle, but in the van means in front, from vanguard, so the wine comes first.
explanation.definitionFit: Redneck, used as an adjective, describes poor rural white Americans as uncouth, much as the slur white trash does.

clue.text: Period before penalties increased sentence?

blocks.note: first meaning: in football, the added half hour played before a penalty shootout
second meaning: a longer prison term, more time to serve

explanation.surface: A judge lengthens a prisoner's stretch before handing out further penalties.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Penalties' and 'sentence' both suggest a court, but the first meaning is football: drawn knockout matches go to added play, then a shootout.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing time is serving a prison term, so more of it is a lengthened term; in football it is added playing periods.

clue.text: Exercise authority having taken lead on project

indicators.note: the lead of a word is its front, so only its opening letter is wanted
having something taken away means losing it, so a letter is removed

blocks.note: an authority on a subject is an expert
the opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: A manager wields power after being put in charge of a project.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Exercise authority' reads as one phrase about wielding power, but the definition is just the first word.
explanation.definitionFit: To exercise strength or influence is to apply it, which is what exerting something means.

clue.text: Heavy burden for ceremonial guards

indicators.note: to guard is to keep something safe inside, so the words hold the answer within them

blocks.note: runs from the end of the first word into the start of the last

explanation.surface: Ceremonial soldiers carry a heavy load of kit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Heavy' looks like an adjective for the burden, but it is a noun: slang for a hired strongman.
explanation.definitionFit: A heavy is a thug employed for muscle, the same as a gang's hired intimidator.

clue.text: Current phone hardware blocks file copy

indicators.note: something that blocks a passage sits inside it, so one piece lodges within another

blocks.note: AC is alternating current
the SIM card inside a mobile phone
taken as written

explanation.surface: Modern phone hardware stops you from duplicating a file.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Current' looks like an adjective meaning modern, but it is electrical current.
explanation.definitionFit: A facsimile is an exact reproduction of a document or object, the source of the word fax.

clue.text: Ordinary Joe is entertaining informally because of witty character

indicators.note: to entertain guests is to take them in, so one piece holds another

blocks.note: an ordinary Joe is an average man; the name is used as written
cos is a casual shortening of because

explanation.surface: An average guy is a fun host because he has a lively wit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Entertaining' looks like being amusing, which suits the definition, but it means holding inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Jocose means playful and given to jokes, so it describes someone with a humorous character.

clue.text: Abnormally large deliveries sealed with adhesive

blocks.note: in cricket, an over is a set of six deliveries by one bowler
size is a gluey wash used to seal plaster or paper, so sized means treated with it

explanation.surface: Huge parcels arrive taped shut.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Deliveries' looks like parcels, but it is cricket: six balls bowled make an over. Size is a gelatinous sealant painted on walls or paper.
explanation.definitionFit: Something bigger than the usual dimensions is too big, in plain English outsize or larger than normal.

clue.text: Wellington’s "cockroach joke" comes between China's leader and Uganda's first couple

indicators.note: to come between two things is to sit in the middle, so one piece goes inside the other two

blocks.note: Mao Zedong, who led the People's Republic of China
to rib someone is to tease or joke with them
the first couple of letters of the country: its opening two

explanation.surface: A joke about cockroaches told in Wellington is placed between Mao and the Ugandan presidential pair.
explanation.walkthrough: Wellington is the capital of New Zealand, not the British duke; 'China's leader' is the whole man, not a first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: In New Zealand the large native wingless cockroach is called by this name, so it is a Kiwi term for that insect.

clue.text: Cave in part of green belt?

blocks.note: first meaning: to collapse or give way under pressure
second meaning: the clasp on a belt, any belt including a green one

explanation.surface: Is there a cave somewhere in the protected countryside around a city?
explanation.walkthrough: The green belt is the protected countryside ringing a British city, which makes 'cave' look like a noun; the question mark admits the belt is just an example and may be any colour.
explanation.definitionFit: Metal buckles under strain when it bends and gives way, and a belt fastens with a clasp of the same name.

clue.text: Departure of vessel put back during slump

indicators.note: putting something back sends it the other way, so the letters run backwards
something happening during a period falls within it, so one piece sits inside another

blocks.note: a ewer is a large water jug
a slump in prices is a fall

explanation.surface: A ship's sailing is postponed during an economic downturn.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Vessel' suggests a ship, which fits departure, but it is a jug.
explanation.definitionFit: A farewell is a leave-taking, the act of saying goodbye as someone goes away.

clue.text: Show listener's support for program

blocks.note: an app is a software program
the ear is what listens

explanation.surface: A radio show proves its listeners back the programme.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Show' looks like a noun, a broadcast, but it is the verb meaning turn up; the 's is just possessive.
explanation.definitionFit: To show up is to arrive or be seen, which is what it means to come into view.

clue.text: "Green" brand of mineral water is withdrawn

explanation.definitionFit: Green describes someone inexperienced and easily fooled, an innocent with no worldly knowledge.

clue.text: Energy multiplied by work equals force

blocks.note: E is the physics symbol for energy

explanation.walkthrough: The physics setting makes 'force' look like a quantity, but it is a verb: to force a payment from someone.
explanation.definitionFit: To exact money or obedience is to demand and obtain it by pressure, which is compelling it.

clue.text: Spinner's average is hard to beat

blocks.note: par is the normal or average level
taken as written
H is the pencil-grade abbreviation for hard
to top a score is to beat it

explanation.surface: A cricket spin bowler's figures are tough to better.

clue.text: Kick around question that goes over one's head

explanation.definitionFit: A toque is a small brimless hat, such as a chef's tall white cap, worn on top of the head.

clue.text: University dons this writer had to mock

the setter speaking of themselves

clue.text: Process to obtain iron perhaps gave off foul fumes

explanation.walkthrough: Both halves sound like one foundry, but the second is the British past tense of a verb about odour.
explanation.definitionFit: Ore is heated in a furnace to extract metal, and in British English something that stank is said to have done this.

clue.text: Dire signs could be characteristic of dead body?
